title: Levered vs. unlevered beta

steps.body: Observed (levered) beta includes two risks: business risk and financial risk from debt.
To compare companies or value a private one: unlever each comp's beta → take the median → relever at the target's capital structure.
Hamada: βU = βL ÷ [1 + (1 − t) × D/E]; βL = βU × [1 + (1 − t) × D/E].

blocks.prompt: Levered beta 1.30, D/E 50%, tax 20% → unlevered beta = **?**
blocks.solution: Levered beta 1.30, D/E 50%, tax 20% → unlevered beta = 0.93 (1.30 ÷ 1.40)

blocks.title: Why unlever and relever?
blocks.teaser: Each comp's beta reflects its own debt level.
blocks.body:
Each comp's beta reflects its own debt level. Stripping out leverage isolates pure business risk, which is comparable across companies. Then you add back the target's own leverage.

**Interview answer:** "Comps have different debt levels, so I strip leverage out to get pure business risk, take the median, and relever at the target's capital structure."

blocks.prompt: Why unlever comparable companies' betas before using them?

options.text: Unlevered betas are always closer to 1.0
Each comp's beta reflects its own leverage; unlevering isolates business risk
Levered betas can't be calculated for public companies
To remove the tax rate from CAPM

blocks.explanation: Strip out each comp's leverage to get pure business risk, take the median, then relever at the target's capital structure.

blocks.title: How do you get a beta for a private company?
blocks.teaser: It has no trading history, so you can't regress.
blocks.body: It has no trading history, so you can't regress. Use the bottom-up method above from public comps.

blocks.title: Why is levered beta higher than unlevered?
blocks.teaser: Debt holders are paid first, so equity holders absorb more of the swings in business value.
blocks.body: Debt holders are paid first, so equity holders absorb more of the swings in business value. More debt → more volatile equity returns → higher beta.

blocks.title: What does Hamada assume?
blocks.teaser: That debt has a beta of zero (debt holders bear no market risk) and a constant debt level.
blocks.body: That debt has a beta of zero (debt holders bear no market risk) and a constant debt level. For highly levered companies, debt carries real risk, so Hamada overstates levered beta. Some practitioners use a version that includes debt beta.

blocks.title: What if a company has more cash than debt?
blocks.teaser: Hamada uses gross debt, so it ignores the cash.
blocks.body: Hamada uses gross debt, so it ignores the cash. But cash has zero beta, which drags observed beta down. A cash-rich company's operating business is riskier than its observed beta suggests. Some analysts adjust for this using net debt or a cash-adjusted beta.
